archetype.name: Game Manager (veteran backup)
archetype.definition: A 14-year journeyman who wins by staying on schedule from structure: quick, short-to-intermediate throws off play-action looks, few risky shots, and steady results only when the script and protection hold up.

report.headline: One tidy start, one rough relief outing: a capable QB3 with a narrow lane
report.take:
Keenum is the Bears' third quarterback. The depth chart has him at QB3 as of late October, and Caleb Williams has started the last two games, so his season so far is two snapshots. In Week 3 he started and beat Philadelphia 27-7: 24 of 34, 247 yards, two touchdowns, no sacks and 7.3 passing EPA. In Week 5 at Green Bay he played a third of the snaps behind Tyson Bagent and went 11 of 19 for 108 yards with an interception, two sacks, a lost fumble and -6.4 EPA. His season line sits around league average only because those two games roughly cancel each other out.

The Philadelphia game shows how he works when things go right. Ben Johnson's offense put him under center a lot. On those 14 plays he completed 92.9% for +0.818 EPA per play, against -0.394 from shotgun. He lived in the intermediate middle, where he gained +0.734 EPA a play on 11 throws, and the pocket stayed clean, with pressure on only 8.6% of dropbacks. That fits who he has always been: low aggressiveness (13.2% tight-window throws), an intended air depth of 7.44 yards, and a career built on timing and structure rather than creation. His one strong NFL season, 2017 in Minnesota, came in a similar play-action, well-supported setting.

The low numbers come mostly from game script and circumstance. The Green Bay relief stint was a mess: he entered trailing in a game that ended 7-31, held the ball 3.08 seconds, and charted a 31.6% bad-throw rate. The trailing-by-9-plus split (-0.568 EPA per play) and the shotgun split are largely that one game. The 4 deep attempts (-0.816 EPA) and the 11 red-zone plays are too few to mean anything. Outside of 2017, his career mostly sits below average in EPA and CPOE. That is the honest baseline for a 38-year-old backup.

Going forward he matters only if two quarterbacks ahead of him go down. If that happens, expect the Philadelphia version in favorable scripts and the Green Bay version when he has to throw from behind. The offense around him ranks 10th in pass EPA, which raises his floor, but he isn't the one who lifts it.

strengths.title: Efficient from under center
strengths.body: Using the run game and play-action, Johnson's scheme let Keenum throw on schedule to defined reads, and he converted almost everything: +0.818 EPA per play on 14 under-center snaps. The sample is small. Still, it matches a career of playing best inside a structured, timing-based offense. That is the role he would be asked to fill again.

strengths.title: Intermediate middle is his zone
strengths.body: Throws of 10-19 air yards produced +0.734 EPA per play, and the middle of the field accounted for both touchdowns. This is the classic veteran-backup skill: anticipating windows over the linebackers rather than driving the ball deep. It is an 11-attempt sample, but it is consistent with how he has always won.

strengths.title: Avoids sacks in clean pockets
strengths.body: His 3.6% sack rate ranks 5th of 45 and he was pressured on only 12.7% of dropbacks. Most of that is the Week 3 game, where he took no sacks and threw quickly. The low pressure rate owes plenty to the Bears' line and play design. The quick release is his.

concerns.title: Falls apart when chasing points
concerns.body: When trailing by 9 or more he produced -0.568 EPA per play. At Green Bay the ball stayed in his hands too long and the throws got loose. A low-aggression passer without a big arm cannot easily throw his way out of a deficit. This is a real limitation of his profile, not just bad luck.

concerns.title: Short game and shotgun underwhelm
concerns.body: Throws under 10 air yards returned -0.108 EPA per play and shotgun dropbacks -0.394. Both are dragged down by the Green Bay stint. Even so, a player of his type needs the quick game to work, and his overall bad-throw rate (17%, 34th of 38) suggests diminished precision at 38.

concerns.title: Career baseline is below average
concerns.body: Outside of 2017 (+0.174 EPA per play), most of his seasons sit in negative EPA territory with below-expected completion rates. One strong start against a defense that now ranks 27th doesn't change that track record.

trend.note: He went from a +7.3 EPA start against a weak Philadelphia defense to a -6.4 EPA relief outing at Green Bay, then back to the bench as Williams resumed starting.

nextGame.headline: QB3 at Seattle: unlikely to play, brutal draw if he does
nextGame.body:
Keenum is the third quarterback and Williams has started the last two weeks, so the base case is that he doesn't take a snap. If he does, it's about the worst setup for his game. Seattle ranks 2nd in defensive EPA and 3rd against the pass. It allows the fewest explosive passes and the fewest QB yards per game, and it hits quarterbacks at the 3rd-highest rate. The one opening is underneath: Seattle is only 21st in EPA allowed on short throws, which is where Keenum would have to work.

On availability, Seattle linebacker Drake Thomas (87% of snaps) is out, which could soften the short middle where Keenum is most comfortable. Drew Lock being out matters only for game script. On Chicago's side, Cole Kmet is on IR and running back Kyle Monangai is out. That leaves more of the tight end work to Colston Loveland and thins the run game that set up Keenum's best play-action work in Week 3.

keyMatchups.title: Seattle's short-zone softness
keyMatchups.body: Seattle is stingy deep but gives up positive EPA on short throws. That is the only part of its defense a 7-yard-aDOT passer can realistically attack. With Thomas out, the underneath middle is the place to go.

keyMatchups.title: Pass rush versus his clock
keyMatchups.body: Seattle hits quarterbacks at a top-3 rate. When Keenum's time to throw stretched past three seconds at Green Bay, everything broke down. He would need the quick game and under-center play-action to survive.

keyMatchups.title: Deep shots are off the table
keyMatchups.body: Seattle allows the least EPA on deep throws in the league, and Keenum's few deep attempts have failed. Any production would have to be built underneath.

nextGame.watch: Williams's and Bagent's health on the injury report: nothing about Keenum's outlook changes unless both are affected.

restOfSeason.body:
Expect Keenum to spend most of the rest of the season as an inactive or emergency quarterback. If injuries push him into a start, the realistic range sits between his two outings. In a balanced or favorable script he can run Johnson's under-center, intermediate-middle offense at roughly league-average efficiency. When forced to chase, he regresses toward his career norm of below-average EPA and loose accuracy.

His Week 3 efficiency (0.213 EPA per dropback) came against a now 27th-ranked defense and won't hold up against good ones. His low sack rate is partly a product of the Bears' protection and will stick only if the line does. The ranges below are per start, should he get one: about 165 to 235 passing yards with one touchdown-ish output.

projections.stat: Pass EPA per dropback (if he plays)

swingFactors: Bears run game health (Monangai) for play-action

confidence.note: Two games, one of them a partial relief stint, and he is QB3 with no clear path to snaps.
